text: Google Cloud revenue doubled, yet the stock fell over 10 percent after hours.
Alphabet's earnings show search queries at a five-year growth high, but search revenue still missed.
Capital spending hit 51.4 billion dollars, pushing free cash flow to negative 9.1 billion.
No buybacks, and 12.4 billion dollars of new shares instead.
Microsoft and Amazon are doing the same, so every AI stock holder should care.
One-time hit, or real trouble in the core business?
First, let's clear out the noise. Alphabet earned 2 dollars and 12 cents a share.
Wall Street expected about 3 dollars. That's roughly 30 percent short.
The biggest drag wasn't the core business.
Alphabet's CFO said its stake in SpaceX fell in value this quarter, so it booked a paper loss.
No cash left the building, so the market usually looks past that.
But even without it, the core business fell short. Operating income was 40.6 billion dollars, about 6 percent below estimates.
Operating margin was 31.8 percent, down two points from the second quarter.
Where did the money go? R&D spending rose 36 percent, driven by AI talent and depreciation.
The cost of the TPU hardware it sells is pushing costs up too.
My take: the market can forgive the drop in earnings per share.
It won't let a miss in core profit slide so easily.
So why wasn't core profit enough? Start with Google's biggest cash machine.
Search revenue was 63.4 billion dollars, up 12 percent. Wall Street expected about 65 billion.
Bank of America's pre-earnings forecast had growth at 14 percent.
YouTube ads brought in 11.2 billion dollars, up 9.2 percent. That missed too.
Together that's 74.5 billion dollars, nearly 60 percent of Alphabet's revenue.
Oddly, people aren't searching less. Sundar Pichai said search query growth was the highest in five years.
The Gemini app has reached a billion users.
So why didn't the money follow? Management gave three reasons on the call.
One, currency. Two, a tough comparison with last year, worth about 3 points of drag.
Three, AI Mode, the chat-style AI inside search. Usage is growing fast, but it earns less than classic search.
The third one matters most. Pew Research looked at this last year.
When a page showed an AI summary, users clicked a regular search result in 8 percent of visits.
Without the summary, it was 15 percent.
Fewer clicks out may also mean fewer chances for ads to earn.
My read: AI isn't making people use Google less. It's making each search earn less.
Currency and tough comparisons will pass. AI Mode's monetization problem won't fix itself.
If you're tracking earnings from the big AI names too, subscribe.
I'm running the numbers on all of them this season.
The old engine is slowing.
So why couldn't Google Cloud, the engine that's supposed to take over, hold the stock up?
Google Cloud brought in 30.7 billion dollars this quarter, up 103 percent.
Operating income was 11.1 billion dollars, and the margin jumped from 23.7 to 36.2 percent.
Wall Street expected about 29.1 billion, growth in the low 90s.
Bank of America was more bullish at 93 percent. So cloud clearly beat.
So why didn't that help? Do the math.
Cloud came in 1.6 billion dollars above estimates.
Search and YouTube together came in 1.8 billion below.
Net it out, and total revenue still missed slightly.
The problem is size. Those two ad businesses made 74.5 billion dollars this quarter. Cloud made 30.7 billion.
For every point of growth ads lose, cloud has to add about 2.4 points to make it up.
Demand isn't the problem. In September, Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said
more than 300 customers had each committed over 100 million dollars.
The cloud backlog hit 561 billion dollars.
The CFO expects just over half of it to turn into revenue in the next two years.
Take that margin with a grain of salt, though. The 36 percent doesn't include the cost of building AI models.
Alphabet books that at the corporate level, and that loss widened from 4.5 billion dollars a year ago to 7.7 billion.
Management also said it's short on its own computing capacity.
It started renting third-party compute late in the quarter and will rent more in the fourth.
Cloud margins will feel it in the near term.
My take: cloud really is sprinting. It just can't carry all of Google yet.
On the revenue side, the old engine is slowing and the new one can't make up the gap.
What about spending? That brings us to the ugliest page in this report: the cash flow statement.
Alphabet spent 51.4 billion dollars on capital expenditures this quarter. That's double last year, and about 40 percent of revenue.
Operating cash flow was only 42.3 billion dollars, more than 11 billion below estimates.
More went out than came in, so free cash flow was negative 9.1 billion dollars.
A year ago it was positive 24.5 billion.
Last quarter it was negative 5.9 billion. That's two negative quarters in a row.
That 11-billion-dollar shortfall in operating cash flow has two pieces worth separating.
One is a one-off. The CFO said Alphabet paid a 2018 EU fine this quarter, 5.2 billion dollars.
The other is TPU inventory. Google builds TPU systems first and gets paid on delivery.
Inventory went from 2.4 billion dollars at the end of last year to 13.3 billion.
The CFO said all of that inventory is tied to signed contracts.
So this quarter's cash flow looks worse than normal.
But the trend of spending more than it earns hasn't changed.
How does it fill the gap? Alphabet issued about 12.4 billion dollars in new shares through an at-the-market offering.
It raised 28.7 billion dollars in debt and bought back zero stock.
It still has 27.6 billion dollars left under that offering program.
Alphabet isn't short of money. It holds 265 billion dollars in cash and marketable securities.
Subtract long-term debt, and there's still about 140 billion dollars in net cash.
But for shareholders, the change is real. The share count used to shrink because profits went into buybacks.
Now debt and new shares are funding the spending, and the share count is growing.
My read: some of this quarter is one-off, but spending more than it earns is going to continue.
Alphabet still has 140 billion dollars in net cash. So why is the market cutting its valuation right now?
This year's capex guidance is unchanged at 195 to 205 billion dollars.
That means the fourth quarter alone needs 63 to 73 billion, more than the third.
And next year? The CFO only said capex will "increase significantly," with details on the next call.
Bank of America estimates around 300 billion dollars. Morgan Stanley put it near 250 billion back in July.
Run Bank of America's number. Over the past 12 months, operating cash flow was about 180 billion dollars.
Now spend 300 billion next year.
Just to break even on free cash flow, operating cash flow would need to grow nearly 70 percent.
And that's only next year. On the call, the CFO disclosed 924 billion dollars in future purchase commitments.
Once signed, those have to be paid.
On the other side is the 561 billion dollar backlog from customers.
But the two don't match. Purchase commitments are fixed.
Whether the backlog turns into cash depends on the customers.
Some of those customers are AI companies like Anthropic, which are still burning cash themselves.
If they keep raising money, Google gets paid on time.
If funding dries up, that risk lands on Google.
That's why the way the market values Google is shifting.
Investors used to see a high-margin, cash-rich platform that bought back stock every year.
Now it looks more like a capital-heavy AI infrastructure company,
and the market pays a lower multiple for the same profit.
That 140 billion in net cash shows Google can pay its bills.
What Wall Street is cutting is how much it will pay for each dollar of profit.
From here, it can go two ways.
If AI monetization in search catches up, and TPUs ship on time and turn inventory into cash,
the market will pay for growth again.
If those signals keep slipping, analysts will have to cut profit estimates, and today's price may not be the floor.
My take: there's real value in Google at this price. But I'm waiting for those two signals first.
To sum up: this drop came from revenue and spending moving the wrong way at the same time.
Each search earns less, cloud can't fill the gap, and spending keeps speeding up.
If you own Google, or any big tech name pouring money into AI, here are the three things I'm watching.
One, the 2027 capex number on the fourth-quarter call.
Two, whether search growth comes back once AI Mode carries more ads.
Three, whether TPU deliveries bring that inventory down.
After this drop, is Google an opportunity or a trap? Tell me in the comments.
